blocks.content: Imagine you are building an app that needs to run on two different cloud platforms AWS and Azure.
Each platform has its own set of services. AWS has S3 for storage, RDS for database, and EC2 for computing. Azure has Blob Storage, Cosmos DB, and Virtual Machines.
The rule is simple everything must come from the same platform. You cannot mix AWS storage with Azure database. That would break everything.
Now imagine doing this without a pattern:
This works for two platforms. But what happens when you add GCP? Or Oracle Cloud? You keep adding more if-elseblocks. Every change risks breaking existing code.
This is the problem Abstract Factory solves.
Instead of scattered if-else blocks, you create one factory per platform. Each factory is responsible for creating its own complete, consistent set of services.
One factory. One platform. Everything consistent.
It is useful when:
["Objects must always belong to the same family.","You need to support multiple environments or configurations.","You want to add new families without touching existing code."]
items: Objects must always belong to the same family.
You need to support multiple environments or configurations.
You want to add new families without touching existing code.

blocks.content: Let's build it step by step.
1. The Problem: Delivery System
Imagine you are building an app that supports two delivery types Standard and Express.
Each delivery type has its own Packaging, Shipping, and Invoice. Everything must match. Standard packaging with Express shipping would cause billing errors and wrong delivery times.
Naive Implementation
Standard Delivery Components
Express Delivery Components
Conditional Client Code
Why This Breaks Down

1. No consistency guarantee Nothing stops a developer from writing new StandardPackaging() with new ExpressShipping(). It compiles fine but the customer gets charged express rates with standard delivery speed.
2. Tight coupling Every file that processes orders needs its own delivery-checking if-else block. Add a new delivery type and you hunt through the entire codebase.
3. No shared interface There is no Packaging type that both StandardPackaging and ExpressPackaging implement. You cannot write a method that accepts "any packaging."
4. Hard to grow Want to add Overnight delivery? Create new classes AND update every if-else block everywhere in the codebase.
5. Violates Open/Closed Principle Every new delivery type forces you to modify existing working code.
What We Really Need

• Group related components by delivery type all Standard components together, all Express components together.
  • One place where delivery type selection happens not scattered everywhere.
  • Shared interfaces so the client works with Packaging, Shipping, and Invoice never with StandardPackaging or ExpressShipping directly.
  • A guarantee that mixing delivery types is impossible.
This is exactly what the Abstract Factory Pattern provides.
2. What is the Abstract Factory Pattern?
blocks.text: 2. What is the Abstract Factory Pattern?

blocks.content: The Abstract Factory Pattern provides an interface for creating families of related or dependent objects without specifying their concrete classes.

The key word is families. Factory Method deals with creating one product at a time. Abstract Factory deals with creating multiple products that must work together. A delivery factory does not just create packaging. It creates packaging, shipping, and invoice that all belong to the same delivery type.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245777056-d498e1e2.png
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245777350-4fa01cfe.png
The Five Participants
In the Abstract Factory pattern, these five participants collaborate to create families of related objects without exposing their concrete classes.
1. Abstract Factory
DeliveryFactory Defines the interface for creating a complete family of related products. Clients only ever talk to this interface never to concrete factories.
2. Concrete Factory

StandardFactory, ExpressFactory Each implements the abstract factory and creates its own consistent set of products. Standard factory only creates standard components. Express factory only creates express components. Mixing is impossible.
3. Abstract Product
Packaging, Shipping, Invoice Define the interfaces for each component type. All concrete products implement these so the client never knows which specific type it is using.
4. Concrete Product
StandardPackaging, ExpressShipping, etc. The actual implementations. Each one contains its own specific logic for packing, shipping, or invoicing.
5. Client

OrderService Works only with abstract factory and abstract product interfaces. Has absolutely no idea which concrete classes it is using. Switch from Standard to Express by changing one thing the factory.
3. How It Works
Here is the Abstract Factory workflow step by step:
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245777489-633217b7.png

Step 1: Configuration determines the factory At application startup, a configuration value or user selection determines which concrete factory to instantiate. This is the only place in the entire codebase that references a concrete factory class.

Step 2: The factory is injected into the client The client receives the factory through its constructor and stores it as the abstract DeliveryFactory type never as StandardFactory or ExpressFactory directly.

Step 3: The client calls factory methods to create products When the client needs packaging it calls factory.createPackaging(). When it needs shipping it calls factory.createShipping(). The client has absolutely no idea which concrete classes are being instantiated behind the scenes.

Step 4: The factory returns compatible products Because the factory is a StandardFactory, every product it returns is a Standard product. There is zero possibility of accidentally getting an Express invoice from a Standard factory.

Step 5: The client uses products through abstract interfaces The client calls packaging.pack(), shipping.ship(), and invoice.generate(). It does not know and does not care whether these are Standard or Express components. The behavior is entirely determined by which factory was injected in Step 2.
4. Implementing Abstract Factory
Let's implement the Abstract Factory pattern step by step using our Delivery System example.
Step 1: Define Abstract Product Interfaces
These are the contracts every delivery component must fulfill. The client only ever works with these interfaces.
Step 2: Create Concrete Products
Each delivery type provides its own implementation of every product interface.
Standard Products
Express Products
Step 3: Define the Abstract Factory
One creation method per product type. Every concrete factory must implement all of them.
Step 4: Implement Concrete Factories
Each factory produces a complete, consistent set of products for its delivery type.
StandardFactory
ExpressFactory
Step 5: Client Code
The client receives a factory through its constructor and only uses abstract interfaces. It never touches a concrete class.
Step 6: Wire Everything Together
The entry point is the only place that references concrete factories. It reads the delivery type, picks the right factory, and injects it into the client.

blocks.content: What We Achieved

• Delivery independence OrderService never references Standard or Express classes directly.
  • Consistency packaging, shipping, and invoice always match the selected delivery type.
  • Open/Closed Principle add Overnight or International delivery without modifying existing factories.
  • Easy to test swap any factory with a mock factory in tests without changing a single line of client code.
5. Practical Example: Payment Processing System

Let's build a payment processing system that supports Credit Card and PayPal payments. Each payment method produces two related objects: a PaymentForm and a PaymentProcessor. Mixing a credit card form with a PayPal processor would break the entire transaction.

blocks.content: Step 8: Adding a New Payment Method
Want to add Crypto payments? Two new product classes and one new factory. Zero existing code changes.
Plug it in. Nothing else changes.

CheckoutService crypto = new CheckoutService(new CryptoFactory());
crypto.checkout("$149.99");

blocks.content: What We Achieved

• Zero mixing risk CreditCardFactory can only produce credit card objects. Pairing a credit card form with a PayPal processor is impossible.
  • Open/Closed Principle new payment method means new classes only. Nothing existing is touched.
  • Clean client CheckoutService never knows which payment method it is using. Swap the factory and the entire behavior changes.
  • Easy to test inject a mock factory in tests without changing a single line of client code.
